source_span: We recommend hedging large geopolitical risks through long exposure to deferred refined products rather than crude, as the outlook on the supply side for refined oil products is more unambiguously negative
source_chain: Mideast/Strait disruption and China's absorption of the shock keep a geopolitical risk premium in crude, and GIR estimates fair value would run $10-15 (or ~$20 per sustained 10% Mideast export cut) higher without the Chinese demand offset and dark-fleet workarounds, therefore the safer hedge is long refined products rather than crude, because the refined-product supply outlook is more clearly negative than crude's. Invalidation: sustained damage to Mideast energy infrastructure/exports that outlasts current dark-fleet and Saudi re-export workarounds, or conversely a real de-escalation that removes the premium GIR is pricing.
pulse_chain: Brent's $16 premium over JPMorgan's $90 fair value prices in 4 million bpd of supply losses that haven't actually occurred, so a ceasefire/diplomacy headline (the Thursday Trump-Xi meeting) can erase the premium instantly, therefore that part of the trade is closing; but diesel is at a record $6.31/gal with refineries already at 97% capacity and no spare capacity to add, so the physical fuel shortage driving inflation persists regardless, therefore the Fed's hiking cycle survives even as the crude premium bleeds out.
why: The pulse attributes the entire fair-value/premium mechanism and every supporting figure ($90 fair value, $16 premium, 4mb/d, 555mb drawn, 1.6bn projected, $6.31 diesel, 97% refinery utilization, 77th-percentile hedge-fund selling) to JPMorgan, but no JPMorgan research note exists anywhere in the day's source corpus (source-text or source-text-all) — the only note in the corpus making a structurally similar crude-premium-vs-refined-product argument is Goldman's (GS Crook/GIR), with entirely different numbers, so this is a bank misattribution compounded by figures that appear in no source document at all.
